readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 15:1-58. This is the great resurrection chapter. Read in four parts: the gospel and the witnesses (1-11), the necessity of the resurrection (12-34), the nature of the resurrection body (35-49), and the victory (50-58). The next two days are doctrinal pauses on this chapter, so today read for the shape of the argument.
settingTheScene: Some in Corinth were saying “there is no resurrection of the dead.” They may have accepted that the soul lives on but not that the body will be raised, a common Greek view. Paul responds with the greatest defense of the resurrection in the Bible. If there is no resurrection, there is no gospel. This chapter is the climax of the letter, and the teaching affects how Christians face death, suffering, and daily work.
observation: “That Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (15:3).
“But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain” (15:10).
“And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (15:14).
“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20).
“For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (15:22).
“The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (15:26).
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” (15:55).
“Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (15:58).
interpretation:
Paul begins with the gospel: “I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved.” Then he gives what is likely one of the earliest creeds of the church: “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.” The resurrection is rooted in history and eyewitness testimony. Paul invites the Corinthians to check with the living witnesses. Notice “in accordance with the Scriptures” twice. The gospel is the fulfillment of the Old Testament.

Then the logic of chapters 12 to 34. If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised; if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is in vain, your faith is in vain, we are misrepresenting God, you are still in your sins, and those who have died in Christ have perished. “If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.” But the truth is “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” The firstfruits is the first part of the harvest, guaranteeing the rest. His resurrection is the start of the general resurrection. The contrast with Adam: “as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.” Then the order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to him, then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule, authority, and power. “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.”

Paul answers the question about the kind of body: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” He uses a seed: what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel. God gives it a body as he has chosen. There are different kinds of bodies, glories of sun, moon, and stars. “So it is with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.” Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust (Adam), we shall bear the image of the man of heaven (Christ).

The climax: “Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.” The dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. “Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law, “but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And the practical conclusion: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.” Because of the resurrection, everything we do for the Lord matters forever.
connection: Luke 24:13-49 and John 20 to 21 describe the resurrection appearances. Acts 2:24-36 and 17:30-32 preach the resurrection. Genesis 3 and Romans 5:12-21 contrast Adam and Christ. Psalm 110:1 and 8:6 are quoted in verses 25 to 27. Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 are quoted in verses 54 to 55. Philippians 3:20-21 describes the transformation of our bodies. 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 describes the coming of the Lord and the resurrection. Daniel 12:2 predicts the resurrection. Revelation 20:11-21:5 describes the final victory.
application:
Memorize 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 as a summary of the gospel.

Think of someone grieving a loved one who died in Christ. Share with them verse 58 or verse 20.

Ask what “work of the Lord” you could do this week knowing it is not in vain.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the gospel of first importance: Christ died, was buried, and was raised.
Tell him what the resurrection means to you.
Ask him to make you steadfast and abounding in his work.
